## Pre-Release v3.13.0 — 2026-08-13 00:12 EDT (#121 · `b19e940`) — the palette stops discarding colours it found, and the refresh path reaches every one

> **Six changes to one subsystem, shipped as one release because each is built on the one before** — the ladder's down-step and its low-colour path both use the selection rule the restrict fix introduced, and the third part is the same root cause at the site the first two exposed. They were developed on separate branches and consolidated before merge; nothing was released in between, so there is no v3.12.0.
>
> **All three are one mistake in three costumes: a quantity that measures COLOURFULNESS being used to answer a question about IMPORTANCE.** It borrowed a pixel-level chroma floor to ask whether an image has colour at all (Part one), let salience collapse to prevalence on an image with no colour to rank by (Part one's truncation), and credited chroma while having no way to say that something is the darkest thing in the picture (Part three) — plus, found while measuring that, normalised a colourless image's own rounding noise to the full accent bonus. Naming the class is what turned the third one from a surprise into the next place to look.

### Part one — the low-colour restrict stops mistaking "unsaturated" for "colourless"

**Harkirat's own server avatar came back with four swatches, no black and neither of its two "rocky brown" shades** — on a picture with visibly more depth than that. The extractor was not at fault: its structure pool had found `#040303`, `#3F342E` and `#28241D` correctly. The **low-colour soft restrict** threw them away, and it did so because it judged "is this image colourless?" by borrowing `CHROMA_FLOOR` — a constant that exists to decide whether a *pixel* is worth putting in the accent pool. 0.04 is a sensible bar for a small punchy feature and far too high a bar for "has colour at all": every sepia photograph, brown avatar and olive banner sits under it while being unmistakably brown to anyone looking. **Having no saturation is not the same fact as having no depth.**

**The gate now reads the PIXEL TAIL against its own floor.** `LOW_COLOUR_CHROMA` (0.01) is checked against the chroma of the image's most-chromatic 3% of pixels. Measured over a 246-image corpus, the old gate fired on 9 images and **4 of them were tinted rather than colourless** — a sepia portrait topping out at 0.027, two brown avatars at 0.033 and 0.037, a dark olive at 0.017. The value is not fitted to that corpus: it is where a colour is, by this module's own `MERGE_DELTA_E` rule, the same colour as plain grey, and the corpus then confirms it is not delicate — achromatic images measure 0 to 0.0031 and the least colourful genuinely-tinted one measures 0.0213, a **7× empty band** around it.

**This also closes the cherry-blossom boundary flip, by construction rather than by moving a threshold.** `tailChroma` is computed from the sampled pixels before a single centroid exists, so it cannot depend on the requested count; the old test read the extracted candidates, which do. Measured at targets 6 and 8: the old gate **disagreed with itself on 3 images**, the new one on **0**. The old rule's stated principle — *judge on the extracted colours, never on raw pixel statistics* — is reversed here, and deliberately: it was right about *aggregate* chroma (a black cat's mean is low while its red eyes are real) but a **percentile** is the very statistic the accent pool already uses to find those eyes. The black cat is still protected, by the same arithmetic that always protected it.

**The truncation was the other half, and fixing only the gate would have shipped it.** When the restrict fires, the four survivors are now chosen by **lightness coverage** instead of by salience — on a colourless image the salience blend collapses to prevalence, so a plain slice returns the four largest regions, which on a greyscale ramp are four neighbouring mid-greys. Before this, a black-and-white avatar kept four near-whites and discarded a real black covering **11%** of the picture; another dropped both `#000000` (11%) and `#111111` (17%) to keep two near-identical light greys. Selection is deterministic farthest-first on lightness — the same traversal the seeding already uses — so the Refresh Colors comparison still holds.

**One defect in the first draft of this fix was caught by measurement rather than by review:** the selection was reading the whole candidate list, including the 50% over-clustering surplus, and picked `#1C1C1C` for a black-and-white avatar — a colour that image's own *unrestricted* palette would never show. A soft restrict must return a subset; showing fewer colours cannot mean showing different ones. It is now bounded by `count` and pinned by a test.

**Verified:** `npm test` green, including a new `scripts/lowColourRestrict.test.js` (12 cases) whose gate assertions were falsification-checked — reverting the floor to 0.04 fails exactly the two cases that should fail. Over the corpus at target 8: 11 of 246 images changed, restricted images 18 → 14, total swatches 1,837 → 1,850, and nothing outside the fired set moved. Harkirat's avatar goes 4 → 8 and regains all three colours it was losing.

### Part two — a second page is never a stub again

**A palette was whatever the extractor happened to find, and 15% of avatars paid for it** — 37 of 246 corpus images rendered a second page holding one, two or three swatches. A stub page reads as broken rather than deliberate. Palettes now land on a **page ladder** of 1, 2, 4, 6 or 8: 1/2/4/6 render on a single page and only 8 paginates. Off-rung counts move to the rung that costs least — `3 → 4`, `5 → 4`, `7 → 8`.

**The first version of this rule was a strict 2/4/8 quota, and measurement killed it before a line was written.** Across the 83 images returning 5/6/7, the honest lever — more seeds, merge threshold untouched, so every survivor stays perceptually distinct — tops out at **22/83 and is non-monotonic** (3.0× is *worse* than 2.5×). The only setting reaching 8 for everyone is `MERGE_DELTA_E` 0.04, which puts a perceptually-duplicate pair in **all 83** palettes and hands back the V3 rewrite's headline win (duplicate pairs 8 → 0). Those colours are simply not in those pictures.

**So the ladder looks harder before it invents anything.** An off-rung count often just means the seeds were spread thinly, so an off-rung palette is re-clustered once at a higher factor and the retry is kept only if it lands on a rung. Measured over 401 images: **35 of the 72 off-rung images land on a rung from more seeds alone** — 20 of 35 sevens reach a real 8, and 6 of 22 fives rise to a clean 6 — needing nothing manufactured and nothing discarded. That leaves **22 images (5.5%)** carrying one derived swatch.

**The CPU worry behind all this turned out to be nothing, and the number that caused it was being read wrong.** The rules file's "palette extraction is 64–183ms" is a whole render phase including fetch and montage pooling. The clustering itself measures **4.2 ms mean at 1.5× and 7.0 ms at 2.5×** on a real 256px source. The retry costs about **4 milliseconds**, on off-rung images only, inside a ~1000 ms cold render. It is deliberately conditional rather than global so the 82% of images already on a rung keep exactly the colours they had.

**A manufactured swatch goes in the palette's emptiest lightness gap**, borrowing hue and chroma from its nearest neighbour so only lightness is new. A blend of two existing swatches was ruled out by measurement: antialiasing seams are kept (they are real pixels), and on a flat two-colour image the seam **is** the blend — re-blending reproduced an existing entry within `MERGE_DELTA_E` in 4 of 5 real cases. A fixed-percentage tint/shade was ruled out too: it degenerates at the extremes, where `tint(#FFFFFF)` is a no-op and `shade(#270100)` lands 0.040 from its base. Targeting an empty slot cannot degenerate that way. If no gap is wide enough, nothing is manufactured — three honest swatches beat four with a twin in them.

**And it says so.** Derived swatches caption as **Synthetic Tint / Shade / Tone**, claimed before every other rule, because every other caption in that vocabulary is a claim about the picture and for this swatch all of them are false. Measured before the rule existed: the 22 derived swatches drew `Edge Detail`, `Deepest Shadow`, `Highlight` and `Warm Accent` — each describing a part of an image that does not contain that colour.

**Nameplates and decorations are untouched.** Their 4 is a ceiling, not a quota — those palettes are a deterministic composition of one bed and three art colours, and padding one would invent a colour for a design that simply has fewer.

**One regression was introduced and caught inside the hour, and it is worth recording because the corpus check could not see it.** The ladder's down-step first used the same lightness-coverage selection the low-colour restrict uses — right for a colourless image, wrong for a colourful one, where it discards a small vivid accent for sitting near another swatch in lightness. Measured on a synthetic control: a **2% pure red on a beige/brown ground was deleted outright**, which is exactly the colour the accent pool exists to surface. The down-step now keeps salience order and drops the tail; nothing is lost, because a colourless image is already on a rung before the ladder sees it. **The 401-image verification passed throughout** — it counted how many swatches came back and never which ones.

**Verified:** 401 images, **zero off-rung palettes**, 22 derived entries and **none within `MERGE_DELTA_E` of a real colour**. `npm test` green, with `scripts/paletteShape.test.js` grown to 23 cases covering the restrict, the ladder, and both regression cases.

### Part three — "the darkest thing in the picture" becomes a fact the ranking can express

**Live testing on the dev bot found a third, separate site of the same chroma-blindness, and it is fixed here.** A server avatar returned a full, healthy 8 swatches whose darkest entry was a dark warm brown, while **the genuine black of the subject's sunglasses was absent entirely**. Nothing was short, nothing errored, the count was already on a rung and the restrict never fired. Harkirat found it by looking at a picture.

**The extractor finds the black perfectly and the slice cuts it.** A clean `#060606` cluster lands at **rank 9 of 9**, because `salience = share/maxShare + SALIENCE_WEIGHT × (chroma/maxChroma)` scores a 1.5% black about 0.05 on the first term and **exactly zero** on the second — and the accent pool that exists to rescue small features cannot take it, since `tailCut` admits only chromatic pixels. **Small and colourless had no path to a slot at all.**

**An additive lightness term is the obvious fix and it was built, swept and refuted.** Across 401 images every shape strong enough to lift a 1.5% black over a 5.5% grey also lifts some dark over some accent — 7 to 14 genuine accents lost at every weight and margin tried, `#380DF3`, `#9907EC` and `#6FE839` among them. **The competition for slots is the mechanism, so no tuning rescues it**; it is the same mechanism the chroma term exists to exploit. So the fix does not compete. `reserveLightnessRange` runs after the truncation and asks whether the palette it just cut still represents the picture's **lightness range**; if an extreme was cut and nothing kept sits within `LIGHTNESS_GAP` of it, one slot is bought back — and the price is **never an accent, never a colour even a structure one, and never the other extreme**, each of those rules bought with a measurement of what happened without it. Accent conservation therefore holds by construction rather than by a lucky parameter, and when nothing may be sold, nothing is bought.

**A second, independent defect surfaced while measuring the first, and it is the same mistake again.** `chroma/maxChroma` is **relative**, so a near-colourless image normalises its own rounding noise to the full accent bonus: on the reproduction, `maxChroma` is **0.0276** — a nearly-neutral taupe — which collected a chroma term of **1.0000**, the identical bonus a **pure red** collects on the same ground. Every mid-grey was being paid the accent premium for chroma that is not there while the real black was paid nothing. The denominator is now floored at `SALIENCE_CHROMA_REF`, which changes nothing on an image whose colours already clear it.

**Verified against a baseline built from `git show HEAD:`, not against an instrumented copy** — over **401 images: 0 accent swatches lost, 1 gained, 36 palettes changed, 0 length changes, 0 off-rung**, and all three real nameplate/decoration assets byte-identical. `npm test` green, `scripts/paletteShape.test.js` grown to **34 cases**, and every new case was proven able to fail by deleting the rule it names — **two were vacuous on the first attempt** and stayed green with their guard removed until the fixtures were rebuilt.

**And live testing the fix immediately exposed why it would not have reached anyone.** Harkirat had to press Refresh Colors **once per source** — on the Avatar page, then again on the Banner page — to see the new colours at all. The cause is not the button: a per-user palette was cached under the **image hash alone**, with nothing recording which algorithm produced it, so after an extractor change every stored palette was stale and nothing could tell. A cache hit needs only a matching hash, and Refresh Colors' own stale-source sweep asks that same question ("has the image moved?") of the other sources, so it correctly skipped every one of them. **Nameplate and decoration were immune the whole time** — their shared per-design palette already carries a `palette_version` in its Cloudinary metadata and heals itself on next view. The per-user cache now carries the same stamp, through **one** identity helper rather than the two independent copies of the rule that existed, since versioning only one of them would leave the staleness test permanently mismatched and re-extract every source on every press. Cost is one extraction per user per source, once, on first view after an extractor change — the same work a cache miss already does, on the lazily-extracted active source only. ⚠️ **`*PaletteSource` now stores `<asset hash>@<algorithm fingerprint>` rather than the bare hash**; no field is added, removed or repurposed, and the fingerprint is a code identifier rather than anything about the user.

### Part four — "Refresh Colors" stops being a per-page chore

Harkirat, pressing the button and watching only one page update: *"it's just unintuitive to make the user press it for global colors and then switch to server colors and press it again."*

**One press now refreshes both views.** A source with a server override caches under its own `guild*` field, so refreshing the server view left the global copy stale and vice versa — one button with two halves, and the user had to go find the other one. The sweep now covers both, and it costs nothing when there is no server profile to sweep: that is readable straight off the interaction payload, so the second pass is skipped outright. Where a source has no override it resolves to the same global image in both views, so the two passes overlap almost entirely and the second one is stopped from paying again for work the first just did.

**It exposed a wrong-pair bug in the same handler.** The accent-cache invalidation chose between the guild and global field pairs using `variant === 'server'` — the view you were *in*, not where the colour was actually cached. A source with no server override resolves to the global image even in the server view, so pressing Refresh there cleared the **guild** accent pair and left the stale **global** one live: no error, and the symptom is an embed that keeps its old tint. It now asks the extractor which pair the source actually used.

**And the confirmation message was rewritten**, to copy Harkirat specified to the character. It leads with **"New colors found!"** and then names what moved under **Refreshed Main Profile** and **Refreshed Server Profile**, each list on its own line, closing with "Everything else is already up-to-date." — the reassurance the whole rework exists to give, since the doubt that started it was *did it do the others?* Two other states: an accent-only refresh keeps its per-source line, and a press that changed nothing says so plainly under its own icon.

⚠️ **The headline is about the PRESS, not about one source**, and that is the substantive fix rather than a wording preference. A sweep that refreshed the banner while the avatar on screen was unchanged is still "new colors found" — reporting it per-source is exactly what let the old message insist nothing had happened while it had quietly updated three other pages. The version it replaces buried the useful part (what else moved) behind a lecture about what the button is for.

It was extracted out of the interaction handler into a pure function so its branches could be tested at all — three states, two per-profile lists, and the decision about which list the *pressed* source belongs in are otherwise invisible until someone presses the button in exactly the right state. **12 cases**, each proven able to fail, including one that mutates the emoji map to prove no value is frozen at `require()` time.

⚠️ One comment was corrected rather than one line of code: the sweep claimed nameplate and decoration "short-circuit on their shared per-design palette, so a stale one is a metadata read rather than an extraction". They do not and never did — the shared palette is resolved for the **active** source only, because resolving it can trigger a whole WebP render. A swept decoration pays a real extraction, ffmpeg included. That is the honest cost of this button, and it is why it carries a 10-second cooldown.

### Part five — the panel's own furniture

**The global/server switch gained its icon**, an animated `ShowColors` matching the eyedropper on Refresh beside it. ⚠️ The id supplied for it was the **dev** application's, and application emoji ids are per-application — the same name is not the same id. The map holds **production** ids as its literal source of truth, so both apps were read live before writing it: prod `1537280503105847486`, dev `1537280678557917275`, with the boot-time name sync re-pointing dev's copy. Writing the dev id would have been wrong in a way that hides, because the sync masks it on every healthy boot and its error path deliberately *keeps* the hardcoded ids — so prod would have rendered a dev emoji exactly when something else had already gone wrong.

**The switch stays grey**, deliberately rather than by default (Harkirat was 50/50 on it). Refresh Colors is the row's one primary action; a second blurple button leaves neither reading as the main thing. The switch is lateral navigation — it changes which colours you are looking at, it does not do work — and its new icon gives it identity without spending colour on the job.

**Download Avatar/Banner stay in the bottom action row.** They were moved into the container for one evening and reverted the same night on sight. ⚠️ The finding on the way is kept because the move will be proposed again: they could never have gone into the heading itself, since a Section carries exactly **one** accessory, a thumbnail **or** a button — a constraint this repo had already paid for once in `/settings` — and the avatar and decoration headings spend theirs on the source's own thumbnail, which is the subject of the page.

**The 40-component ceiling is now asserted rather than remembered.** Exceeding it is a hard send failure this bot has already taken as a production crash, and the panel had only prose standing between it and the next addition. A full avatar page measures **30 of 40** and a banner page **31**, and the test asserts real headroom rather than merely being under the line — a page sitting at 39 passes a ceiling check and crashes on whatever anyone adds next.

### Part six — Accent Color Style drops to three options, and Dynamic gets a real pool

**Five styles became three: Pre-Designed Palette, Avatar Color, Dynamic Profile Colors.** Banner Color and Display Name Colors are retired — both already fell back to Avatar whenever their own source was missing, and neither earned a slot. Checked against production before removing them: `accentColorStyle` held **avatar ×17 and preset ×1**, and not one document carried either value, so this strands nobody. A stored value is still **normalized** rather than deleted, because the field is a plain String with no enum and nothing stops an old one existing; unnormalized it would resolve against a source the UI can no longer offer.

**Avatar Color needed no change at all** — it already used your server avatar where you have one and your global avatar otherwise, decided per source by where you ran the command, with DMs always global. That is `getCachedColor`'s existing behaviour and it is also why there is deliberately no stored "which profile" setting.

**Dynamic Profile Colors now draws on every swatch you have saved**, across both your main and server profiles — up to 8 avatar + 8 banner + 4 nameplate + 4 decoration, rather than one colour per source. Display Name Colors are excluded: they are exact values picked in Discord's own UI, not colours extracted from an image.

⚠️ **The fallback is the whole design, not a safety net.** `*Palette` fields are written **only** by the View Colors panel, so a user who has never opened `/colors` has no stored swatches at all — measured on production, **12 of 18 preference documents (67%)** had none. A pure swatch pool would therefore be empty for most people and fall through to the preset, i.e. an option that appears to do nothing, silently. So a source with no stored palette contributes its single accent colour exactly as before, and the pool gets richer as you browse your own colours. Extracting on demand to fill it was **rejected rather than overlooked**: up to four extractions, ffmpeg included, inside a command render is precisely the synchronous CPU burst that caused the bot-wide `10062` interaction timeouts on 2026-07-13.

⚠️ **One test in this batch was VACUOUS and was caught by the standing habit of deleting each rule to watch its case fail.** Two of the pool cases exercised a *copy of the expression written inside the test file*, so removing the server-profile half of the read and removing the malformed-entry guard both left the suite green. The reader was extracted into an exported function specifically so the test reaches the shipped code. A test of a re-implementation reports on the re-implementation.

## Pre-Release v3.11.0 — 2026-08-12 14:09 EDT (#119 · `06db012`) — the swatch captions stop asking "than what?"

**Harkirat rejected the shipped label set in four words: "what is 'IT'???"** — *cools it down · cuts against it · warms it up · sets the tone · fills the space · backs it up · adds depth · opens it up*. Every one is a verb phrase whose object is an antecedent the caption never supplies, which is the same defect as the earlier "Lighter Version" (than what?) rejection wearing a verb instead of an adjective. The register is now **self-contained noun phrases**, and the test is blunt: read a caption alone, with no other swatch visible, and if it makes you ask "than what?" it is the rejected pattern again. `Catches the Eye` survives only because "the eye" is the reader's own.

**It shipped as a VOCABULARY rather than a fourth flat set of labels, and that shape came from how Harkirat kept answering.** Given a menu he chose *two* words per rule and said when each applies — on soft vs muted: *"soft implies lighter, gentle, whites, greys, baby pink, powder blue… muted implies matte, sophisticated, darker, slate blue, dusty rose."* So a rule now decides which **role** a swatch plays and a variant, chosen from that swatch's own chroma and lightness, decides the **wording**: `Prominent`/`Backdrop`, `Warm Accent`/`Warm Trace`, `Wild Card`/`Outlier`, `Undertone`/`Deep Tone`, `Loud Accent`/`Vibrant Accent`, `Soft Accent`/`Muted Accent`, `Harmonic`/`Neighboring Shade`/`Muted Harmony`/`Neutral Shade`, `Vivid Echo`/`Echo`/`Quiet Echo`, `Brightest Point`/`Palest Tone`/`Lightest`. One caption, two facts.

**`Synergetic Hue`/`Synergetic Shade` names a relationship the old rules called a mistake.** At 150–210° of hue with real colour on both sides, two colours are COMPLEMENTARY — they reinforce each other — so `Outlier` framed a deliberate scheme as an oddity. It has to outrank the temperature rules to speak at all: a complement is almost always the opposite temperature too, and while `Cool Accent` claimed those swatches first it fired **once in 889**. `Cool Accent` was not wrong there, just vaguer, and the more specific true thing wins.

**A 246-image corpus was built as a falsifier, and it found six classes of caption that were simply false.** `local/colors-investigation/label-corpus.mjs` labels 1,837 real swatches in ~0.2s from a cached extraction. It caught: a colour covering **46% of its image** captioned as a small feature (`Pop of Color` had no size ceiling at all — accent-pool membership says a colour is chromatic, never that it is small); `Quiet Echo` on a neon orange-red; `Harmonic` on greys with no hue to harmonise with; `Stray Color` on near-blacks; and a hue claim made about two greys 130° apart, where hue is meaningless. All now measure zero.

**And it exposed a real extractor bug that predates the labels: palette percentages summed past 100%.** Pool B (accent) clusters a subset of the pixels Pool A already clustered, so a colour winning a centroid in both had its two shares added at merge — 92 of 246 palettes summed over 100%, the worst to **155%**, with two single entries over 100% on their own. Every sampled pixel is now assigned to its nearest final centroid and shares recomputed, so each is counted exactly once. Colour sets barely moved (207 of 246 identical), but **12 palettes changed which colour holds index 0** — the slot that is a contract.

**Verified:** `npm test` green (68 docs-audit self-checks, paletteAlgoVersion 17, animatedMediaPipeline 5, accentCache 7, 26 hook tests, reflow 29). Zero dangling referents, zero false claims across six classes, zero duplicate captions on a page, zero null labels. The nameplate bed path, palettes with `origin` stripped (the older cache wire format — 246 palettes, **zero throws**, which finally tests that documented invariant) and degenerate palettes were all exercised.

## Pre-Release v3.10.0 — 2026-08-11 23:23 EDT (#118 · `39dcf0e`) — the message and the side effect finally agree

**Refresh Colors told the truth about the wrong thing.** Its "no change" message compared palette bytes only, and never accounted for its own unconditional accent-cache invalidation — so a user who opened View Colors (which already force-refreshes the palette on open) and then hit Refresh Colors got told "still generates the same colors" on the exact click that actually fixed their stale accent, because the palette itself had nothing left to find. The message now distinguishes "palette unchanged, but the accent was stale and just got refreshed" from a genuine no-op.

**A second, separately-reported symptom traced to no code defect at all.** The same live session produced a report that View Colors showed a stale avatar/palette on FIRST open, updating only after an explicit Refresh — with both calls going through the identical `forceRefresh: true` path. Traced the whole chain (`getCachedPalette`'s cache-hit shortcut is gated `if (!forceRefresh && ...)`; the guild profile comes from `interaction.member` directly, not a locally-cached copy) and found nothing wrong on our side. Documented as a likely Discord CDN propagation-lag incident in `.claude/rules/accent-and-colors.md`, for reference if it recurs.

**The low-colour restrict is confirmed chroma-blind, and it's worse than the boundary-flip symptom already on file.** Instrumenting `getColorPalette` directly on a real avatar showed the structure pool correctly finding a genuine black cluster and two dark browns — discarded anyway, because the truncation judges "low colour" purely by chroma and never checks lightness spread. Filed for its own design session (`P2 · M · Opus5-High`), superseding the older cherry-blossom boundary-flip item rather than sitting beside it.

**Built the instrumentation to answer the third question with data instead of screenshots.** `models/RenderTiming.js` + `utils/renderTiming.js` now time every View Colors panel action and both WebP cache modules' cold-render path, into a collection that a Cloudinary/Discord-channel dev-cache purge can't touch — the exact kind of data this investigation lost partway through. Filed as its own session (`P2 · M · Sonnet5-High`) once enough real clicks have accumulated.

**Process, not code:** cleared the one stale `avatarPalette` field (test account, scoped) predating the current extraction algorithm; disclosed `RenderTiming` in `docs/legal/PRIVACY.md` per the `privacy-model-coverage` gate; added `deferred-list-model-tag-check.sh`, an advisory hook flagging a filed/edited deferred-list item with no model+effort tag, after three items shipped without one in this same session.

**Verified:** `npm test` green (accent-cache 7/7, reflow-prose 29/29, hook self-tests 26/26 including the new one), `docs:audit` clean, dev bot reloaded cleanly under `--watch` after every edit.

## Pre-Release v3.9.0 — 2026-08-11 21:10 EDT (#117 · `26ee06a`) — the model-selection grid stops being a pointer

**A rule that turns on specific values cannot be enforced by naming where those values live.** The session-start gate requires a model + effort recommendation "picked from the grid in `reference_priority_tier_system`". Three layers already said so — `docs/SESSION-START.md` (auto-loaded), the `MEMORY.md` index line (auto-loaded), and the `UserPromptSubmit` hook itself (fires every turn). All three were in context, and the recommendation was still made from a remembered shape of the table: **twice, wrongly, in opposite directions** — first over-specced to `Opus5-Medium` for a live-verification pass, then over-corrected to `Sonnet5-Low`, a cell Harkirat had already retired in writing.

**The diagnosis is the useful part: a pointer preserves the CONCEPT and drops the DISCRIMINATING VALUES.** "premise-risk × deliberation-load grid" is enough to feel informed and not enough to be correct. It carries neither axis definition nor the retired-cell rule — and those two facts are exactly what both wrong picks turned on. Axis B in particular means **how many PLACES** (`Low = one place · Med = several · High = many sites`), not how hard the thinking is, which is what let a phrase like "moderate taste load" inflate the first pick. Whose judgement it is never enters the lookup at all.

**So the table moved to where the decision is made.** The inline `UserPromptSubmit` echo became `.claude/hooks/self-check.sh`, which now carries both axis definitions, all twelve cells, the retired-cell floor, the one-cell-never-a-range rule and the event-driven escalation triggers. **No file needs opening and no memory needs trusting.** ⚠️ It is knowingly a **second copy** of content the `reference_priority_tier_system` memory owns — duplicated state that can drift — and that trade was made with eyes open, because the alternative is a pointer and a pointer is the thing that measurably failed. The memory is named in the hook as canonical, and `self-check.test.sh` pins the values that actually discriminate (axis definitions, four corner cells, the retired-cell rule), so drift fails the suite rather than a session.

**Harkirat's framing is what forced the right fix, and it is worth quoting because the first two attempts were both non-fixes.** After a correction was written into the memory file: *"so you edited a memory file, which you admitted you didn't even read until i explicitly flagged it, to improve your behavior about using and reading that specific memory file? make that make sense."* It didn't — a "read the file" instruction, filed in a file that has to be read, about a failure consisting of not reading files. **Adding a fourth pointer is not a fix; it is the same non-fix in a new location.**

**Verified:** `self-check.test.sh`, 15 cases, and **proven able to fail** — breaking one grid cell fails exactly that assertion and no other. Hook coverage 25/25 (every script in `.claude/hooks/` has a test), full `npm test` green, `docs:audit` clean.

## Pre-Release v3.8.0 — 2026-08-11 15:19 EDT (#116 · `e885c8a`) — the palette stops paying for a picture nobody looks at

**The montage was being PNG-encoded purely so it could be decoded again one function call later, and that round trip is gone.** `poolFramesIntoMontage` builds its sampling sheet as a Jimp image, then returned it as PNG bytes; `getColorPalette` immediately called `Jimp.read` on those bytes. Nothing in between stored, uploaded or looked at that PNG — it existed only to cross a function boundary. `getColorPalette` now accepts an already-decoded image (duck-typed on `.bitmap.data`, since Jimp 1.x builds instances through its own plugin wrapper and an `instanceof` check is the brittle way to ask "is this decoded"), and the montage hands its image over directly. **Measured on three real assets: 28ms saved on the 43-frame twilight nameplate, 56ms and 84ms on two real 60-frame decorations — with the extracted palettes verified byte-identical before and after, on every one.**

**The tiles are now copied into the sheet row by row instead of composited, which is both the faster option and the more accurate one.** That ordering is the opposite of how a hand-rolled blit usually reads, and it is the point: compositing "source OVER a fully transparent destination" is mathematically the source itself, so nothing in this step ever needed blending. Jimp's `composite()` runs the full over-operator regardless, and its integer rounding hands back source ±1 on every partially-transparent pixel — **13,134 altered bytes on the twilight sheet and 67,175 on a real decoration, all of it error introduced by a blend that had nothing to blend against.** On that decoration the error was large enough to move an extracted swatch: `#117AF1` → `#127BF2`, **and the copy's value is the correct one.** Harkirat's question when the tradeoff was put to him — *"can't you utilize the blitz but fix the rounding issue?"* — has a tidier answer than expected, because the copy **is** the fix. Measured **83–98ms → 0.5ms**. A guard falls back to `composite()` if a tile is ever sized differently from the first, since the grid geometry is derived from `tiles[0]`; every frame of one animation is identical, so that path is insurance rather than live.

**A decoration's frames also stopped being written to disk twice.** ffmpeg writes each frame into a temp dir; the old path read all of them into memory, deleted that dir, and then wrote the identical bytes back out into a *second* one because `img2webp` reads real files rather than stdin. In the common no-resize case nothing touches a pixel in between, so `extractAlphaFrames` gained an opt-in `asPaths` mode that leaves the frames where they are and hands back a `cleanup()`, and `encodeWebpFromFrames` now takes paths as readily as Buffers. On a 60-frame decoration that removes **60 writes and 51 reads** — the palette montage samples only 9 frames, so the other 51 were being read purely to be discarded. It stays opt-in because the nameplate render genuinely needs every frame's pixels to composite its bed, and because handing the caller ownership of a temp dir is a real cost, paid in a `finally`. The encoder also stopped creating a temp dir of its own when the frames already share one — **2 → 1**, which was the second half of the item's stated verify condition and was very nearly shipped unmet: the first pass measured *leaked* dirs (zero, correctly) rather than dirs *created*, which is a different property, and every test was green either way. This was a filed `P3 · XS` whose own condition was *worth doing only if that path is being touched anyway*; it was, and Harkirat's call was to fold it in. ⚠️ It is no longer quite free: `extractAlphaFrames` is an input to the palette key, so even this byte-identical refactor moved the key and re-derived every stored palette to reach identical colours.

**A decoration render also stopped decoding a whole frame to answer a question the first 24 bytes already answer.** The resize branch needs only the source dimensions, and ffmpeg's extracted frames are plain PNGs whose IHDR chunk carries width and height at fixed offsets. `readImageSize()` reads them there and falls back to a real decode on anything that is not a PNG, so it can never be the reason a render fails. Verified against `Jimp.read` on 12 real frames across both source formats.

**Honest framing on the headline number, because the obvious reading of it is wrong.** The palette work did not *add* ~350ms to a render — v3.7.0 moved extraction **into** the render from `colorPalette.js`, where it had been paying a separate asset fetch and its own ffmpeg pass. The render's own timer simply started covering work that used to happen elsewhere, and total work went down. What this release removes is genuine waste inside that step: **the pooling phase drops from ~130–190ms to ~51–61ms**, roughly **145–167ms off a cold decoration render and ~46ms off a nameplate**, with no change to what the extractor sees beyond the rounding correction above.

**A stored palette now records which algorithm produced it — as a hash DERIVED from that algorithm, not as a version number anyone maintains.** This is what makes the correction above land everywhere rather than only on designs nobody had viewed yet, because the per-design cache keys on the asset hash and an asset hash does not change when an extractor does — the same trap the per-user colour caches already carry a memory about. `palette_version` goes into Cloudinary `context` beside the palette and is **read back as a gate: a palette tagged with anything else is treated as absent.** Absent is already what both caches route through their heal path, so a stale entry re-derives itself in place on next view — **no purge script, and none wanted**, since deleting the resource would take the render and its `discord_cdn_url` with it.

**The first version of this shipped as the string `v3.8.0-pre` and Harkirat rejected it on the right grounds:** *"there's a unique versioning for the actual algorithm."* A hand-written release tag fails in **both** directions and neither failure announces itself — it only moves when someone remembers, so a real algorithm change can ship under a stale tag with every cached value quietly wrong; and naming it after a release invites bumping it every release, re-deriving identical output for nothing. `utils/algoFingerprint.js` now hashes the code itself: the clustering functions and their helpers, the eleven constants that shape the output, and the montage builder. **Shipping v3.9.0 or any later release does not change this value and forces no re-derivation** — it moves if and only if that code moves. Comments and whitespace are stripped before hashing, which is not cosmetic in a codebase this comment-dense: hashing raw source would invalidate every cached palette every time someone clarified a sentence. It errs toward over-invalidating (renaming a local changes the hash) because the failure modes are not symmetric — a false invalidation costs one metadata re-derive, a missed one leaves a wrong value cached forever behind a marker swearing it is current.

**Deciding what counts as "the algorithm" is the whole design, and the first pass drew the line too tight — twice.** A stored palette depends on the *pixels* every bit as much as on the clustering, so the hash reaches upstream of the extractor: `poolFramesIntoMontage` decides which frames are pooled and how they land on the sheet, and `extractAlphaFrames` decides which frames exist at all. Fingerprinting `colorExtract.js` alone would have missed **this release's own tile-copy fix**, which moved a swatch while touching nothing in that file. The second miss was subtler: the ffmpeg **fps and decoder flags** live in the two cache modules, differ per media type, and cannot be imported into the hash without closing a cycle — `-c:v libvpx-vp9` is what makes a nameplate's alpha survive at all, and `-f apng` is what stops ffmpeg silently reading a 60-frame decoration as one still. Each cache now folds its own `FRAME_OPTS` into the key at the call site, which also collapsed four inline copies of those options into one per module. Nameplates and decorations consequently carry **different** keys, as they should.

**Verified live against the real dev cache, which is where the whole story closes.** Both production folders hold **zero** resources — every render made so far lives in the dev-scoped namespace — so the existing entries could be reset with nothing user-facing at stake. The decoration whose swatch the rounding had moved came back **`#117AF1` → `#127BF2`**, the corrected value; then each key change invalidated the entries again and they re-derived, ending at `3b59f9396188` for decorations and `b8b9117fa480` for the nameplate. **`discord_cdn_url` survived every one of those patches** — the specific thing that breaks if `context` is written in two calls instead of one. A fourth entry (cat-beans) was left untouched because the test harness guessed its asset URL wrong and got a 404: **the heal degraded exactly as designed**, returning the cached object unchanged rather than writing a partial context, and it will re-derive on its next real view where the URL comes from Discord's own payload.

**`scripts/paletteAlgoVersion.test.js` (13 cases, wired into `npm test`) pins both directions**, because every failure mode of this key is silent and a test that only checked "the hash is a string" would pass under either. A comment rewrite and a reindent must **not** move it; a changed body, a changed constant, and a different montage fingerprint **must**. The round trip is pinned too: a palette tagged by another algorithm, one with no marker at all, and a malformed one all read back as absent, and an empty palette writes no marker rather than a marker with nothing under it.

**Refresh Colors now also drops the accent colour, so the button finally does what its name says.** It had been re-extracting swatches while every embed across `/calendar`, `/draws` and the rest kept its old tint — the accent lives in a different cache and `getCachedColorFromUrl` has no `forceRefresh` path at all, so no caller could bypass it. `invalidateAccentCache` clears the accent pair for the source on screen and for every stale source picked up in the same press. It **invalidates rather than recomputes**: an accent colour resolves on the next accent-using command anyway, so clearing the field guarantees a fresh value without spending CPU inside a button press, and costs a `'preset'`-style user nothing. It clears the **guild pair or the global pair, decided by the view being refreshed** — never both, because those pairs exist so that moving between a server and a DM does not have each context evict the other's colour.

**The accent ALGORITHM was re-examined against the day's work and deliberately left alone — this is the entry to read before "finishing the job" later.** Harkirat's question was whether it should inherit the palette rewrite. Verified first: it is entirely HSL-based (24 hue bins, `s < 0.15` filters, `weight = s²`) while the palette moved to two-pool OKLab, so it does carry the same saturation flaw the label layer was fixed for. **Kept anyway, on measurement.** Across the corpus the current accent sits a mean **ΔE 0.037** from the nearest real palette swatch, **10 of 11** within the merge threshold — the tint on an embed is nearly always a colour `/colors` actually shows you. A chroma-based rewrite was then built and **rejected on its output**: it changed **6 of 10** images visibly, moved `cinnasip.png` from a pale pink to `#4D5395` — the very dark navy the open over-saturation item is about — and left one image with **no colour at all**, its chroma floor having excluded every pixel. The lesson is the useful part: **HSL's inflated saturation at high lightness is, for this job, a feature.** It biases the accent toward light, prevalent colours, which is what a single embed tint wants; chroma biases toward small punchy regions, which is what a palette wants. Same flaw, opposite correct answer.

**Refresh Colors now picks up every source whose image actually changed, not just the one on screen.** Harkirat's design: change only your banner and you pay for the banner; change your avatar, banner and nameplate and you get all three, while the two you left alone cost one string comparison each. The staleness test is free — every image hash is already in hand from the call the panel makes anyway to build its nav buttons — so the only work done is for sources that genuinely moved. The follow-up names what else was picked up, because the panel renders one source at a time and a silently-updated Banner would otherwise look like nothing happened. ⚠️ **This is not a return to the pre-2026-07-13 "extract everything on every render" behaviour that caused the bot-wide `10062` interaction timeouts** — it runs only on an explicit button press, only for genuinely stale sources, behind that button's existing 10-second cooldown.

**The nameplate cache message was redesigned to Harkirat's own spec, and the accent is now the bed colour.** He wrote the layout out line by line; it is reproduced in the rules file and matched to the character. The shape is what keeps it compact: **only the heading is body-size**, carrying the design name and the output metrics (`### Cat Beans — 512×96px · 26f · 226.7kB`), with palette, asset, Cloudinary id and render time all dropping to small text beneath it. The palette name and its four hexes are one line because they are one fact — and since `palette[0]` **is** the bed, the first hex is the bed and the separate Bed field disappears rather than printing the same value twice. The accent change reverses his own earlier "first art colour, not the bed" call: the bed is the entire background of the rendered nameplate, so it is what the design reads as at a glance. The decoration message follows the same shape, **derived rather than specified** — a decoration has no name, no palette name and no bed, so its heading is the metrics alone.

**Superseded within the same release, and worth saying so plainly:** an intermediate four-line `**Label:**` layout shipped earlier the same afternoon on the reasoning that grouping was the win. It was — but it was still my grouping, not his, and the version that matters is the one the person reading these messages every day asked for.

**Two things that were first written up as "latent traps no check can see" got fixed instead, and the reasoning error is worth more than the fixes.** Harkirat's response to the write-up was *"why was that even sidelined or not properly documented OR NOT FIXED ALTOGETHER?"* — and the write-up had confused two different claims. They could not be **observed** by an existing check; that is not the same as being **unable to be made checkable**, which is what "document it" quietly assumed. (1) `extractAlphaFrames` selected frames with `startsWith('frame_')` from a directory the encoder now also writes `out.webp` into — safe only by accident of the name. One `FRAME_FILE_RE = /^frame_\d+\.png$/` now both writes ffmpeg's output pattern and reads it back, so they cannot disagree. (2) The montage's non-uniform-tile fallback to `composite()` would have produced **different colours from the same code** — and a source-derived cache key cannot see a runtime branch — so it now **throws** instead; unreachable for a real caller, and both call sites already degrade to no palette rather than a failed render. `scripts/animatedMediaPipeline.test.js` pins both, including a hostile `frame_out.webp`.

**Nameplate public ids lost two thirds of their length.** `dev_nameplate_webp/nameplates-nameplates-twilight-cobalt` is now `dev_nameplate_webp/twilight-cobalt` — Discord serves every nameplate under `nameplates/nameplates/<design>/`, so the repeated segment was a constant nobody had questioned. Only that exact three-segment shape is shortened; anything else keeps the full slug, since a tail segment is only unique when its parent is known-constant. ⚠️ The public id **is** the cache key, so this orphans anything stored under the old name — done here precisely because both prod folders held zero resources and the dev entries were purged and re-rendered in the same pass.

**Cold-render cost, measured after the purge — and the honest reading is that this release barely moved the nameplate path.** The dev cache was emptied and all four designs re-rendered from cold: Cat Beans **1007 → 968ms**, Twilight **1870 → 1757ms**, and the 60-frame decoration **905 → 823ms** with its palette phase going ~350ms → 183ms. So the savings landed where the work was: **the decoration path.** On nameplates, palette extraction is now only 64–116ms of the render, and **`renderGradientBedFrame` is 63–71% of it** — 611ms and 1240ms respectively, roughly 24–29ms per frame of Jimp compositing. That is the next real hot spot and it is filed as its own item; further nameplate speedups have to come from there, not from the extractor. ⚠️ Single runs, and the fetch component varied 24–132ms across them, so the phase shape is the reliable part rather than the totals.

**Verified:** `local/colors-investigation/pipeline-parity.js` runs the shipped `poolFramesIntoMontage` end to end against three real Discord assets and compares its palette against both the old encode→decode path and an independent reference implementation of each variant — the round-trip removal is byte-identical on all three, and the shipped output matches the row-copy reference exactly. Modules boot-loaded; `readImageSize` cross-checked against a full decode on 12 real frames.

## Pre-Release v3.7.0 — 2026-08-11 13:27 EDT (#115 · `5ba533c`) — a design's colours computed once, and named like a person would

**Nameplate and decoration palettes are now cached per DESIGN rather than per user.** Harkirat's observation, filed at the end of the previous session: the extractor is deterministic, so a nameplate's palette is a pure function of `(asset, palette)` and a decoration's of `(asset)` — identical for every user who equips that design, forever. Re-deriving it per user was work with a known answer. The palette is now computed **inside the WebP render**, from the frames that render already holds, and persisted in the same Cloudinary resource's `context` metadata beside `discord_cdn_url`. Any later viewer of that design gets the colours with no extraction at all.

**It removes duplicated work rather than adding a layer.** Nameplate extraction had been re-fetching the `.webm` and re-decoding frames the render had just produced; those are now one pass. It also **removes a circularity**: the storage-channel message's accent colour used to be passed *into* the render from a palette extracted separately upstream, so the render depended on an extraction over the very frames it was holding. The render computes its own palette, so that parameter is gone.

⚠️ **The render must extract from the RAW frames, never the composited set** — the bed is composited onto every frame immediately afterwards, and extracting from those would reintroduce exactly the bed contamination v3.6.0 removed. Verified by parity test against the real twilight asset: the palette computed inside the render is **byte-identical** to the one the old separate path produced (`#0131C2 #2962E5 #4289E7 #1A2156`, 43 frames), and re-running is deterministic, so Refresh Colors' change-detection is unaffected.

⚠️ **The wire format is deliberately not JSON.** Cloudinary encodes `context` as `key=value|key=value`, so a value containing `=` or `|` corrupts the whole map. Palettes serialise as `RRGGBB:PP,...` — hex digits, colons and commas only — and a malformed value decodes to `null` rather than a partial palette, since a half-decoded palette would render as a real one.

**A design rendered before this shipped heals itself on next view.** Its WebP is already cached and would never re-render, so it would have fallen back to per-user extraction forever. Those backfill their palette once — metadata only, no re-render, no re-upload, and the existing cache-channel message is left alone.

**The cache-channel embeds now carry the four hex codes** (Harkirat's explicit ask), alongside the existing Asset / SKU / Palette / Bed / Dimensions / Frames / Size lines.

**Two regressions found while wiring this, both shipped by earlier versions and neither previously noticed:**

- **The nameplate cache message's accent colour had silently become the bed.** The line read `palette[0].hex` under a comment stating "Majority extracted color, **NOT bedHex**" — accurate when written, but v3.6.0 changed the composition to prepend the bed at index 0, so the code began doing precisely what its own comment forbade. With a bed present the first art colour is index 1. On twilight that is `#2962E5` rather than `#0131C2`.
- **Guild-profile nameplates lost their design name and SKU in the cache channel** — a server-profile nameplate posted headed "Nameplate" with no `SKU:` line while a global one posted correctly. ⚠️ **The filed root cause was wrong**, and the entry's own "traced, one step short of proven" caveat is what stopped it being applied blind. It attributed the loss to a snake_case/camelCase shape mismatch; in fact `readGuildProfile` computed `decorationSkuId`, `nameplateSkuId` and `nameplateName` correctly and then **never returned them** — all three were missing from the returned object literal, so every read of them was `undefined` regardless of payload shape. A computed-but-unreturned local is invisible to callers *and* to any search for the field name, which is how it survived a review that read the derivation and assumed the plumbing. Found by a test asserting the returned value.
  - The shape bug was nonetheless **real, just not this symptom's cause.** discord.js renames keys *inside* the object it rebuilds, so a `GuildMember` carries `skuId`, never `sku_id` — the shipped "dual-shape" fallback read the snake_case spelling under *both* branches and resolved to null in every guild the bot has joined. `asset`, `label` and `palette` survive the transform unrenamed, which is why they came through and masked it.
  - ⚠️ **The `label` field and its parser were never at fault.** `deriveNameplateName` remains the primary source of a design's name, re-confirmed live against the real payload. A fallback deriving the name from the asset path (`nameplates/nameplates/cat_beans/` → "Cat Beans") was added only for a payload carrying no label at all, since that would otherwise head a *permanent* cache entry as the generic "Nameplate". It never fires on either known asset. Its first version happily minted `"A0ff7f9be49be57356dd3cf0d9c02605"` from a hash-shaped asset — caught by its own test, now rejected.

**Swatch names were rebuilt around a third vocabulary, and both of the old selection rules turned out to be defects.** Harkirat's read after seeing the plain-English names live: "Peach" and "Dark Peach" are too flat, and `#FDBE74` reads as "Warm Apricot" or "Cantaloupe Cream". The target register is **evocative but transparent** — you can picture the colour without knowing the reference — and it sits between the two things he had already rejected ("Rajah" too obscure, "Peach" too flat).

⚠️ **The vocabulary was not the main problem. Two selection rules were.** (1) Naming still matched in **RGB** while the whole V3 extractor had moved to OKLab — the naming layer never got the memo. Fixing that alone cut mean corpus error **32%** and worst-case **by half**, with no vocabulary change at all. (2) A "simplest name wins" tiebreak, added for a single case (`#FEFEFE` picking "Pale Grey" over "White") that no longer exists, scored candidates by `words × 1000 + length` — so `#FDBE74`'s genuinely nearest match **"Apricot" (ΔE 0.030) lost to "Peach" (0.039) on a two-character difference.** It was a blandness filter wearing a correctness costume, and it is gone.

**Wikipedia's "List of colors" joins as the preferred vocabulary** (812 names, vendored at 20.5 KB) ahead of XKCD and ntc. It is the only obtainable list holding the target register — "Mellow Apricot", "French Violet", "Terra Cotta", "Bright Lilac" exist in no other list checked.

⚠️ **"Bigger is better" is measured FALSE, and this is the finding worth keeping.** Against 54 real names sampled from a reference app: `color-name-list` at **31,914 entries reproduced 3 — worse than a list 35× smaller** — because at that density crowd-sourced novelty ("Crown Chakra", "Fake Love", "Azuremyst Isle") sits nearer to any given colour than the established names, making the good ones unreachable. Its 4,959 and 3,082-entry cuts scored **zero**. The union of **all 46 vocabularies published on npm** tops out at 15/54, so the reference app's list is not obtainable; that was chased to the end and should not be re-chased.

**Selection is now three rules.** The preferred list wins unless another is closer by a **perceptually real** amount (`MARGIN` 0.02) — an absolute gate was tried first and is wrong, since at 0.03 `#730BC8` fell through to ntc's "Purple Heart" (0.040) over "French Violet" (0.044), trading the register for 0.004 of invisible accuracy. And a **base-word dedupe** rejects a repeated *last word* within one palette, because "Persian Blue / Tufts Blue / Clear Blue / Royal Blue" has four distinct names and is still unreadable — corpus distinct-base went **83% → 99%**.

**"Basically White" / "Basically Black" are removed** (Harkirat's call). They existed only because the 908-name vocabulary had nothing between "White" and a grey; with Wikipedia in the pool `#FDFDFD` names itself "Baby Powder". Exact `#FFFFFF`/`#000000` still return "White"/"Black" naturally.

⚠️ **ΔE cannot see the quality this whole change is about** — "Mellow Apricot" and "Macaroni and Cheese" both score ~0.02 against `#FDBE74`, so every accuracy table in this investigation was blind to the exact complaint that started it. Two strategies that scored the *name* rather than the distance were built and **rejected on their own output**: a "self-describing" ranker won its metric **93% vs 47%** and produced "Texas Rose" and "Fire Bush"; a quality-tiebreak hybrid was tested at four window sizes and came out identical to the shipped rule on both nameplates, worse elsewhere, and at the tightest window named `#FDFDFD` plain "White". **Judge future changes here on real palettes, never on a metric alone.**

**Measured across 20 corpus images / 135 extracted swatches**, against what shipped this morning: mean perceptual error **0.0282 → 0.0184** (−35%), worst case **0.1703 → 0.0489** (−71%), swatches whose name describes a visibly different colour **4 → 0**, distinct base words **99%**. On the real Cat Beans nameplate: `Violet · Lilac · Dark Peach · Peach` → `Violet · Bright Lilac · Dark Peach · Mellow Apricot`.

**The swatch LABELS were rebuilt around what a colour does, after two rejections.** Harkirat rejected a first pass outright — *"improvement doesn't mean slap on more words… the way it classifies, the way it phrases, the intuitiveness, the uniqueness, the expansiveness, the relevance"* — and then rejected a second, which is where the real pattern surfaced: **every label he disliked was a comparison to a swatch that isn't on screen.** "Lighter Version" than what; "Same Family" as what; "Across the Wheel" of a colour wheel the reader cannot see. The ones that worked were all verb phrases that stand alone, so the rest were converted into that register.

⚠️ **Rank is no longer a labelling rule at all.** "Most Common" meant *it is first in the list* and "Second Most Common" meant *it is second* — the reader is looking at the order, so those captions carried **zero** information and could not be fixed by renaming. Index 0 now reads **"Sets the Tone"**, which says what dominating an image actually means.

**The extractor's accent pool now reaches the label layer, which needed real plumbing rather than new adjectives.** `getColorPalette` runs two pools, and an accent-pool entry is by construction a small high-chroma *feature* — the cat's red eyes, the gold sparkle. That fact was computed and thrown away at merge. It now survives (sticky toward `accent`), rides through the Cloudinary palette cache in the wire format, and drives **Catches the Eye** / **Pop of Colour** — the only labels here stating something statistics cannot recover. ⚠️ Pool membership alone is not enough: the accent pool is the most chromatic tail *of its own image*, so a first build labelled a sepia photo's beige "Catches the Eye". Both rules now also require the colour to beat the palette's median chroma.

🐛 **And chasing one odd label surfaced a real bug that predates all of this.** A pale pink on a white avatar was labelled "Turns It Up", i.e. more saturated than the dominant. Measuring why:

```
#FDFEFE  (white to any eye)   HSL saturation = 0.333
#020311  (black to any eye)   HSL saturation = 0.789
```

HSL's saturation denominator collapses as lightness approaches its extremes, so a few units of RGB drift read as 79% saturated. **Every colourfulness threshold in the label function had therefore been meaningless for near-whites and near-blacks since it was written** — two of the commonest swatches there are. All 13 judgements now use OKLab chroma, which behaves identically at every lightness. It improved the labels as a side effect: `Deep Cerise` on a white avatar went from "Adds Depth" to **Catches the Eye**, which is what it actually is. ⚠️ Chroma's range is ~0–0.37, not 0–1 — a saturation threshold pasted across without rescaling is wrong by roughly 3×.

**Measured: 17 categories across 135 corpus swatches with ZERO fallbacks** (one before the chroma fix). On Cat Beans: `Nameplate Background · Fills the Space · Warms It Up · Catches the Eye`.

**Hosted swatch images were considered and rejected — on a measurement, not an argument.** The open question was whether serving the per-swatch PNGs from Cloudinary would beat generating them per render. The previous session asserted the encode was "cheap" without ever putting a number on it. Measured: a cold encode is **0.43 ms** (median 0.36, worst 1.5), a warm memo hit is **0.4 µs**, and a swatch PNG is **181 bytes** — so a full 8-swatch page costs **3.5 ms and 1.4 KB**. Hosting would trade that for permanent per-hex Cloudinary assets and Discord's external-media proxy re-encoding every reference. Not worth building.

**Verified:** parity and determinism against the real twilight asset · wire format round-trips including the bed's `percent: 0` entry, rejects every malformed input, and contains no Cloudinary-hostile character · all three member shapes (raw payload, `GuildMember`, `GuildMember` with no label) resolve a real name and both SKUs · full hook suite 24/24 · docs audit clean. ⚠️ **Not yet verified in Discord** — a cold render against the live cache channel still needs a dev-bot pass, and the v3.6.0 naming/label changes have themselves never been seen in a live panel.

## Pre-Release v3.6.0 — 2026-08-11 09:12 EDT (#113 · `ec39820`) — animations sampled whole, small colours surfaced, and names people actually use

**Two defects, both measured against a 22-image corpus of real avatars and banners Harkirat supplied**, rather than tuned against the one picture that started the investigation. The scripts, the classifier masks and the before/after comparison sheets are in `local/colors-investigation/`.

**The animation bug is the one with the largest blast radius, and Harkirat predicted it from a source GIF before it was measured.** `extractFrameMontage` selected frames with a **hardcoded stride of 3** into a 9-tile grid, so it only ever saw frames **0..24** no matter how long the animation was — its own comment claimed it "spans the whole cycle", which was true only for animations of 27 frames or fewer. Measured on a real 85-frame banner whose pale sky blooms into crimson flowers after frame ~34: **a single frame loses 83% of the image's peak chroma, and the old montage lost 84%** — that is, the montage was no better than the single frame it was written to replace. **This also silently shortchanged the 60-frame decoration case it was originally built for.** Two further traps in the same function: `-f apng` was hardcoded as the demuxer, which ffmpeg needs for APNG but which **rejects a GIF outright**; and the montage was only ever wired to decoration, so **animated avatars and banners still extracted from a single static CDN frame**. Stride now comes from a real `ffprobe` frame count, the container is sniffed from the bytes, and animated avatars/banners route through the montage. ⚠️ Frames are now also **scaled before tiling** — a 3x3 grid multiplies source resolution ninefold, and a 999×427 animated banner tiled out to **3.8M pixels** for a synchronous Jimp decode, which is precisely the event-loop stall behind the historical bot-wide `10062` wave. Verified: crimson recovered at distance 2.2 from the measured target, montage 29× smaller, and a black-and-white GIF still returns chroma exactly `0.0000`.

**The palette extractor's "asked for 8, got 6" had a single root cause, and the two obvious suspects were both refuted.** Seeds were chosen by sorting pixels by hue and taking every `n/k`-th **by index**, which allocates them by pixel *population* rather than colour coverage — and since `rgbToHsl` reports hue `0` for every neutral, a large dark region collapses onto one hue position. On the avatar that prompted this, **10 of 12 seeds landed in two regions and only 10 were even distinct**, leaving skin, highlights and a yellow feature with no seed at all. ⚠️ **Empty clusters (0 dropped) and merge chaining (0 of 6 merges were chain-only — a non-chaining merge produces byte-identical output) were both measured and ruled out; they are not worth re-litigating.** Replaced with deterministic **farthest-first seeding**, clustering in **OKLab with lightness down-weighted** so a greyscale ramp cannot monopolise the seeds, and merging in **true, unweighted OKLab** so "two swatches must differ perceptually" is one honest promise instead of a side effect of a tuning knob.

**The real prize is the accent pool.** A colour region covering ~1% of an image can **never** win a slot under prevalence ranking, no matter how vivid — which is why a black cat's **red eyes**, a holographic avatar's **orange and pink**, and a cartoon's **yellow eyelids** were all absent. The most chromatic few percent of pixels now get their own clustering pass, free of competition from the background; rendered classifier masks confirmed that tail lands *exactly* on those features. ⚠️ It **self-disables on greyscale** through an absolute chroma floor, so no colour can be invented where there is none.

**Low-colour sources now soft-restrict to 4 entries — judged on the EXTRACTED colours, not on raw pixel statistics, and that distinction is the whole design.** By aggregate chroma a black cat scores as "low colour" and would lose the very red eyes this work exists to surface; judged on its extracted palette it keeps its full allowance because it genuinely has an accent. It fires on 4 of the 22 corpus images and correctly leaves the cat alone. ⚠️ The previous behaviour was **inconsistent rather than principled**: juul's banner returned 4 while a pure black-and-white ink banner returned **8 near-identical greys** — the "correct 4" was substantially luck.

**Target stays 8 with 4+4 pagination, and that is a height decision, not a count one.** Harkirat's call: 4 entries per page already takes considerable vertical space, so 6-on-a-single-page would read *taller* than 8-across-two.

**Verified:** perceptual duplicate pairs across the 22 images went **8 → 0**; juul's eyelid yellow, the cat's red eyes and the holographic orange/pink all now present; both pure-greyscale banners return 4 entries at chroma `0.0000`; determinism confirmed by double-run comparison, so Refresh Colors' change-detection is unaffected; full hook suite 24/24. ⚠️ **Not yet verified in Discord itself** — this needs a live dev-bot pass over `/colors` for both the `|g` and `|s` variants.

**Nameplate extraction never saw the bed, so its swatches came from unbacked translucent art.** ⚠️ To be precise about the user-visible part: the panel *was* already surfacing the bed, appended as a **fifth** entry after the four extracted colours (2026-08-09). So nobody was missing that colour — what was wrong is that extraction spent all four of its slots on art it was reading without a backing, and the fifth entry tipped the page into a needless `1 / 2` pagination. Harkirat pointed out that Discord's `static.png` and `asset.webm` carry only the nameplate's **upper layer**; the background "bed" is a CSS gradient the client draws from the design's palette metadata. Measured against the real twilight asset before writing anything: `static.png` is **0.0% opaque** (32.9% fully transparent, 67.1% partial alpha), confirming no bed is present in the bytes. Extraction was therefore reading translucent art with nothing behind it. A new `renderNameplateExtractionMontage()` pools evenly-spaced frames from the `.webm`, composites the gradient bed onto each, and tiles them into one still. On the real twilight/cobalt pairing the palette goes from `#336CED #5B96F1 #1E4DE9 #83C5F4` to `#0738C6 #1D56D6 #2E73DC #4D90E9` — the same hue family, but grounded in the bed the user actually sees rather than washed out by unbacked alpha.

⚠️ **A claim in the first draft of this entry was WRONG and is corrected here rather than quietly edited away.** It said the same art ships for every palette, so extraction returned an identical palette for lemon, crimson and clover, and that "a crimson nameplate reported blue". **That cannot happen.** A nameplate's art and its bed are a **linked design** — the palette is metadata describing which bed Discord renders for *that* design, not a free choice a user makes over arbitrary art (Harkirat, 2026-08-11 07:42 EDT). The three-palette comparison was a **synthetic probe** forcing twilight art onto beds it never ships with; it demonstrated that the code was bed-blind, which is real, but it was never evidence of a user-facing colour mismatch. The fix stands; the justification was overstated.

**The four nameplate swatches are now one background plus three from the art, and there is no "Majority Color" among them.** Harkirat's call: with only four slots a majority statistic doesn't earn one, and the background is a design fact rather than a measurement. Entry 0 is labelled **"Nameplate Background"** and carries the bed's hex **exactly** — `nameplatePaletteHex` already knows it, so extracting it from pixels could only approximate a value we hold precisely. The remaining three come from `renderNameplateArtMontage()`, which pools evenly-spaced `.webm` frames (art only, transparent backdrop) so a colour that appears part-way through the animation still counts; the caller over-asks by two and drops any art colour within `MERGE_DELTA_E` of the bed, so a near-duplicate never costs a slot. Measured on twilight: cobalt → `#0131C2` + `#2962E5 #4289E7 #1A2156`, crimson → `#900007` + three art blues, both with entry 0 exactly equal to the bed.

Designs whose palette is `none` already have their background baked into the art, so they get no prepended bed and take all four from the pooled art — nothing is invented.

**Colour names stopped trying so hard, and the swatch labels followed them.** Harkirat's read: names like "Rajah" and "Robin's Egg Blue" were straining for uniqueness. Naming now prefers the **XKCD colour-survey vocabulary** — crowdsourced from what ordinary people actually call colours — falling back to the old "Name That Color" list only when no plain name is close enough or the good one is already taken on that page. The nameplate bed outranks both and uses **Discord's own palette word** ("Cobalt", "Violet"). So `Bunker, Yellow Sea, Pirate Gold` became `Almost Black, Yellowish Orange, Mustard Brown`, and `Japonica, Rajah` became `Dark Peach, Peach`.

The **labels** were plained up in the same pass, since name and label are read together on one line and "Almost Black / Dark Undertone" mixed two registers: `Majority Color → Most Common`, `Dark Undertone → Darkest Tone`, `Vibrant Accent → Boldest Color`, `Secondary Color → Second Most Common`, `Complementary Tone → Opposite Hue`, `Balanced Tone → Similar To Main`. The rules that assign them are unchanged; only their wording is.

⚠️ **The obvious version of this is a trap, and it was measured rather than assumed.** Switching to the CSS colour names *collapses* palettes — 148 names cannot separate eight shades of one image: across 146 real swatches they produced **19 duplicate-name pairs affecting 12 of 22 images**, one avatar reading "black" three times in eight slots, against the old list's 3. XKCD's ~900 names beat the incumbent on **both** axes: plainer **and** fewer collisions (**1 duplicate pair** corpus-wide). A wider library survey was run at Harkirat's request and rejected on **fitness, not licensing** — `color-name-list` (MIT) names these same colours "Eigengrau", "Dream Vapour", "Bacon Strips", "20000 Leagues Under the Sea".

⚠️ **The list is VENDORED (22.5 KB), not a dependency, and that was measured too.** `color-name-lists` ships all 36 vocabularies in one 2.05 MB JSON retaining **6.90 MB of heap**. Harkirat asked whether just the one list could be pulled instead — it can — that package exposes each list as its own file, at 0.18 MB — but it still drags **8 transitive dependencies** that this repo's rules require attributing and copyleft-auditing, for frozen 2010 survey data. Vendoring the cleaned list costs 22.5 KB and no dependency at all.

⚠️ **A public survey spells things how people typed them, and 54 entries had to go or be corrected.** 28 crude joke names ("shit brown", "diarrhea", "piss yellow") sitting squarely in the olive band a khaki avatar reaches, 11 with slashes, 2 uselessly vague — plus 13 spelling and language slips found by scanning the whole list rather than patching what surfaced: `Liliac → Lilac`, `Purpleish → Purplish`, `Greyblue → Grey Blue`, and the non-English `Azul`/`Rosa` dropped. One further fix came from a near-tie: `#FEFEFE` is visually white, but "Pale Grey" sat 0.3 RGB closer than "White" and won, so near-ties now go to the **simplest** name.

**"White" and "Black" are now reserved for the exact values.** They're the two names a reader takes literally, so a swatch that is merely *near* them reads as though the panel rounded off — and near-black is the common case, since extraction averages a whole dark region. `#FFFFFF` is "White"; `#FEFEFE` is **"Basically White"**. `#000000` is "Black"; `#010101` is **"Basically Black"**. Both forms can appear in the same palette without colliding.

⚠️ Harkirat caught a collision in the proposal before it shipped: a **Violet** bed alongside an art colour whose nearest name is also "violet" would have printed "Violet" twice. Names are assigned across the whole entry set in order, so Discord's authoritative name claims its word first and the art colour falls through to "Lilac".

**⚠️ Still open, filed rather than fixed:** Harkirat's observation that because the extractor is deterministic, nameplate and decoration palettes are pure functions of `(asset, palette)` and should be cached **globally and permanently** rather than per-user — the same key the WebP cache already uses.

## Pre-Release v3.5.0 — 2026-08-10 23:31 EDT (#112 · `8e0c794`) — `/help` gets real, clickable slash-command mentions

**Every command Dioreo can reference now becomes a real, clickable slash-command mention** (`</name:id>`) instead of plain backtick text — click one and it types straight into your chat box, no more copy-typing `/settings` by hand. Harkirat found the format in Discord's own docs and tested it by hand first (a mention placed in the dev bot's own bio); the trickiest part isn't documented well: a subcommand or subcommand-group mention (`/draw prices`, `/patch notes`, `/season end`) still resolves off its TOP-LEVEL command's id — there is no separate id per subcommand, and a wrong one fails completely silently, rendering as plain text with no error.

IDs come free: `index.js`'s existing command-registration call to Discord already returns every command's real id in its response, so `client.commandIds` is built straight off that with no extra API request. A new `utils/commandMentions.js` resolves the mention at render time, matching the convention `utils/emojiMap.js` already uses for emoji ids — a value that only exists after the bot is connected to Discord must never be frozen into a module-level constant, since the dev and prod bots are separate Discord applications with different ids for identically-named commands.

Landed in `/help`'s landing directory and every detail page's command heading, plus six spots elsewhere in the bot where one command's text names a sibling command (`/draw prices` and `/calendar`'s "check out /settings" tips, `/server`'s two `/settings` mentions, `/manage`'s `/autobuild` pointer, `/autobuild`'s own retry/expiry messages, and `/alerts`' admin-only rejection). One genuine platform wall found along the way: a slash command's OPTION description (the grey helper text Discord shows while typing) is not message content and never renders markdown or mentions — `/calendar`'s `[view]` option keeps its plain-text `/settings` reference for that reason, while the near-identical wording inside `/help`'s own body (real message content) became a live mention. `/help`'s Examples lines (option-value syntax, e.g. `weapon:AK117`) are intentionally untouched — a mention can't pre-fill an option value, and Harkirat parked that one for a later pass rather than a hard no.

**Verified:** boot-tested on the local dev bot; Harkirat confirmed `/help`'s landing page, every detail page including the three subcommand cases, and all six cross-reference spots render as real clickable pills in Discord.
